title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
hook: Martin Luther King Jr, jailed, writes to fellow clergy that injustice in one place threatens justice in every place

segments.voice: Yesterday: Billy Graham, an old hymn, and ropes coming down. Your line: just as I am.

A cell in the Birmingham city jail. A pastor has been arrested for leading a march in defiance of a court order. A newspaper reaches him, with a public statement from a group of white clergymen in the city. They call the demonstrations unwise and untimely. They say outsiders are stirring up trouble, and the right course is patience and the courts. The pastor has no desk and not much paper. The story goes that he starts his answer in the margins of that very newspaper, and on scraps smuggled in and out. The pastor is Martin Luther King Jr., writing to fellow ministers.

The letter is full of the Bible and the church. To the charge that he was an outsider, he answered that he was in Birmingham because injustice was there, and compared himself to the apostle Paul, who left his home town to carry the gospel to other cities. Then a claim readers still quote: injustice in one place is a threat to justice in every place. In his picture, all people are bound together in a single garment of destiny, so a tear in one part runs through the whole cloth. To the charge that the time wasn't right, he wrote that for Black Americans the word wait had nearly always meant never. On breaking laws, he reached back to Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, saints of the church, to argue that an unjust law is no true law at all, while insisting that anyone who breaks one must do it openly, lovingly, and accept the penalty. He reached for the prophet Amos too. In the King James Bible: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Not a trickle, saved for a better season. A river. Some of the letter's sharpest words aren't aimed at open enemies, but at the white moderate, who agrees with the goal in principle and keeps asking for patience, and at white churches that stood by. King wrote with grief about the church, not against it. He was a pastor, disappointed in his own house, and he still called it home.

Think of one unfairness close to you that isn't happening to you: a coworker always talked over, a neighbor without a ramp, a school rule that lands harder on some kids. Look at it plainly, notice the part of you that says it's not the right time, and find one small, honest word you could say. If you pray, hold Amos's line about justice running down like water.
Birmingham, where Martin Luther King Jr. wrote from a cell to fellow clergy who had told him to wait.
Your line: justice is all one piece. One garment of destiny. Nine hundred sixty days now.

howItsDone: Some Christians read King's letter in churches, classrooms and study groups, and some congregations read parts of it aloud together.

fork.setup: you're in a jail cell, and fellow ministers publicly call your work unwise and untimely. what do you do?
options: write them a long, careful answer, minister to minister.
attack them by name in the press.
fork.reveal: King wrote a long reply to his fellow clergy, full of scripture and church teaching, answering each charge in turn.

chat.says: King was told to be patient and wait. Why didn't he?
options: He wrote that for Black Americans, wait had nearly always meant never; justice couldn't be put off.
He thought waiting was fine, but the march was already planned and couldn't be stopped.
He had given up on the church, so the clergymen's advice no longer mattered to him.
chat.meaning: King answered that for Black Americans wait had nearly always meant never. With Amos, he called for justice to run down like waters.

Amos.meaning: a Hebrew prophet who called for justice

white moderate.meaning: King's term for people who backed the goal but urged waiting

apostle Paul.meaning: the early missionary who carried the gospel to other cities
